title: Trump Administration Announces More Than $5 Billion for the Genesis Mission, a National Mission on AI for Science
key_claim: More than $5 billion in federal commitments and more than 15 federal agencies now sit behind the Genesis Mission, whose named challenges include building autonomous laboratories for self-driving experimentation across scientific domains.
frame_summary: The White House argues that AI-for-science requires a national mobilisation on the model of past great programmes, with shared federal infrastructure and agency-pooled datasets as the vehicle, and positions autonomous laboratories as one of the mission's named national challenges.
verbatim_quote: autonomous laboratories that leverage robotics, edge AI, and real-time analysis to enable self-driving experimentation at unprecedented scale across scientific domains
verbatim_list: Today, Assistant to the President and Director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Michael Kratsios unveiled more than $5 billion in Federal commitments expanding the Genesis Mission alongside new mission-driven National Science and Technology Challenges.
More than 15 Federal agencies will contribute research awards, funding opportunities, specialized scientific datasets, and research facilities to the National Science and Technology Challenges.

title: Secretary of Energy Chris Wright Announces First Genesis Mission Projects Selected to Accelerate AI-Driven Scientific Discovery
key_claim: DOE selected 278 projects across 342 participating institutions, including 157 companies, and awardees gain access to the Genesis Mission Platform of AI agent frameworks, models and national-laboratory computing.
frame_summary: DOE frames the first Genesis awards as evidence that the American research community is ready to reorganise around AI-enabled workflows, and presents platform access rather than cash alone as the substance of the award.
verbatim_quote: The Genesis Mission RFA generated the largest response to a funding opportunity in DOE history.
verbatim_list: 278 awards: 87 led by DOE and National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) National Laboratories, 168 led by universities, 19 led by companies, and 4 led by nonprofit organizations.
342 participating institutions: 16 DOE and NNSA National Laboratories, 142 universities, 157 companies, 13 nonprofit organizations, and 14 other institutions.

Awardees will gain access to the Genesis Mission Platform, including AI agent frameworks, advanced AI models and software made available through industry partners, and high-performance computing resources across DOE’s National Laboratories and partner facilities.

title: AI in Science (Working Paper 34953), Ajay K. Agrawal, John McHale and Alexander Oettl
key_claim: AI raises scientific productivity as an augmentation tool rather than through full automation, with returns that vary sharply by domain and by workflow stage, and with human judgement indispensable where data are sparse.
frame_summary: The paper argues that AI enters the knowledge-production function as a search amplifier over combinatorial spaces, so gains are uneven across domains and stages and depend on complements such as skills and organisational design rather than on the technology alone.
verbatim_quote: across domains (e.g., data-rich biology vs. anomaly-sparse physics) and workflow stages
verbatim_list: We decompose knowledge production into a multi-stage process to shed light on the "jagged frontier" of AI in science

title: Why AI cannot do good science without humans (Editorial)
key_claim: In both flagship multi-agent discovery studies published in Nature, humans framed the project and ran the physical experiments; the FutureHouse team estimated its Robin system cut project time 200-fold against a typical human workflow.
frame_summary: Nature argues that the new multi-agent discovery systems empower rather than replace human researchers, because humans still frame problems, run experiments and check output, and because tacit team expertise may not be reproducible by machines.
verbatim_quote: humans framed the initial project, performed experiments, offered guidance and checked the agents’ output along the way
verbatim_list: The team estimates that Robin reduced the time needed for the project 200-fold compared with a typical human workflow.
The experiments Robin suggested were then handed over to humans, who conducted the studies and fed the results back to Robin for analysis, interpretation and the design of follow-up studies.

title: Agentic AI Scientists Are Not Built For Autonomous Scientific Discovery (arXiv:2605.08956)
key_claim: Agentic AI systems function as co-scientists but are not built for autonomous discovery, in part because training corpora omit the tacit procedural and failure knowledge of laboratory practice and benchmarks lack feedback from physical experiments.
frame_summary: The position paper argues that the shortfalls of autonomous AI scientists are inherent to current training and deployment choices rather than fixable by scale, so the human-specified problem, dataset and success criteria remain load-bearing.

title: Scientists using LLMs will 'do more, less well', modelling study predicts
key_claim: A modelling study posted on arXiv on 19 July 2026 predicts that LLM adoption will push scientists to start new projects rather than refine existing ones, producing more papers of lower quality.
frame_summary: Nature reports the modelling result as evidence that AI acceleration interacts with existing publication incentives, so faster discovery phases translate into more output rather than better work unless the incentives change.
verbatim_quote: Adoption of LLMs will cause scientists to “do more, less well — rather than the same amount, better”, write the authors.
